h: פּוּרִים, מַאֲמָר ו׳ Purim — Maamar Vav

p: פּוּרִים עַל שֵׁם הַפּוּר [אֶסְתֵּר ט, כו].
Purim, after the name of the Pur" (Esther 9:26).
At first glance we must understand
after the matter that was the trouble,
And why did they not name the days
עַל שׁוּם שֶׁפָּסַח וְכוּ׳ [פְּסָחִים קטז, ב]
and in the Torah, the Festival of Matzos,
עַל שׁוּם שֶׁלֹּא הִסְפִּיק בְּצֵקָם וְכוּ׳
because their dough did not have time, etc.
"for I made them dwell in sukkos," etc.,
All are named for the time of the Exodus and the redemption,
belongs to the time of the decree.
was itself for the good of Yisrael,
for the Pur of Haman was transformed into our Pur.
רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי פָּתַח וְכוּ׳
"And it shall be, as He rejoiced," etc.,
"so will He rejoice to do you harm."
at the downfall of the wicked?
Behold it is written, 'As they went out,' etc.,
'for it is good' is not said
לְפִי שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שָׂמֵחַ
because HaKadosh Baruch Hu does not rejoice
at the downfall of the wicked;
"'The work of My hands is drowning in the sea,
but He causes others to rejoice," etc.
"And when they were liable to annihilation in the days of Haman,
what is the connection of this opening
to explain the matter of the Megillah,
and this has no connection at all
and what difference does it make
that He causes the enemies to rejoice, according to Rashi's explanation?
Also, why was it necessary to write in the Torah
that He causes the enemies to rejoice?
Surely this is not part of the punishment,
for what difference does it make
וְגַם מַה שַּׁיָּיךְ עַל זֶה הַדִּמְיוֹן
And also, how does the comparison apply here:
so how can one compare it
and say "so will He rejoice," etc.?
Also, what they asked in the Gemara,
וּמִי חָדֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא וְכוּ׳
"But does HaKadosh Baruch Hu rejoice," etc.,
why did it need to bring proof
from the fact that "for it is good" is not said
since that verse is about the war of Yehoshafat
וּמִדְּרָשָׁא דְּלֹא קָרַב זֶה אֶל זֶה
and from the derashah of "one did not come near the other,"
and there it speaks of the Egyptians?
Are there not many explicit verses
"In all their distress He is distressed,"
and our Sages of blessed memory said
but rather 'He is righteous and saved':
as it were, He is saved,"
the Shechinah was exiled with them,
'For your sake I was sent to Bavel';
and when they are redeemed, the Shechinah is with them,"
"'And He will bring back' is not said,
So we see that HaKadosh Baruch Hu,
as it were, suffers in their distress;
that He would rejoice, chas v'shalom,
But behold, in the Torah it is written,
how can one say regarding Yisrael
Was not the entire world created
and also for the sake of the Torah
and if, chas v'shalom, to destroy,
that He would blot out the name of Yisrael
"If the heavens can be measured," etc.,
all the offspring of Yisrael," etc.
So how can one imagine, chas v'shalom,
But we find in Yitzchak's words to Esav:
"And it shall be, when you grieve,
that you will be pained over the blessings
why it is written "And it shall be,"
for our Sages of blessed memory said
that "vehayah" is an expression of joy;
The expression "vehayah" would have been more fitting
However, I heard from our holy Rebbe,
may the memory of the holy tzaddik be for a blessing,
for the life of the World to Come,
that when the time of Esav's downfall arrives,
then he afflicts and distresses Yisrael the most,
and immediately he has a downfall;
and this is what it says, "when you grieve,"
at the time of his downfall,
"and you shall break his yoke," etc.
On the contrary, he will distress Yisrael,
and immediately his downfall will come
and therefore it uses the expression "vehayah,"
for then it is joy for Yisrael.
And the culmination of his downfall comes
at the time when the holiness of Yisrael increases.
And before the giving of the Torah
there was the war of Amalek,
that Yisrael were destined to receive the Torah,
and the kelipah of Amalek grew strong
and immediately he had a downfall:
וַיַּחֲלוֹשׁ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ אֶת עֲמָלֵק וְגוֹ׳ [שְׁמוֹת יז, יג].
And Hashem Yisbarach aroused him to this
in order to weaken his strength,
for he is "the first of the nations"
and the power of the yetzer hara,
as they said in the holy Zohar
and he must be weakened and brought down
before the giving of the Torah,
Yisrael will be prepared for it.
the increase of the holiness of Yisrael,
for then there will be the ultimate perfection
and therefore then there will be aroused
the war of Gog and Magog,
for our Sages of blessed memory said
"Gog and Magog has the numerical value of seventy,"
For he will gather all the seventy nations,
and the root will be through Esav,
that the son of David does not come
from the verse "until the time that she who is in labor has given birth";
and the birth pangs of Mashiach
are like the pangs of childbirth;
וְאָז יִהְיֶה בֵּית עֵשָׂו לְקַשׁ [עוֹבַדְיָה א, יח]
and then "the house of Esav will be straw" (Ovadiah 1:18),
which "the coming day will set ablaze,"
and there will be the complete erasure of Amalek,
"and there will be no survivor," etc. (Ovadiah ibid.);
so that all evil will be consumed,
And so it was with Purim:
that the kelipah of Amalek sensed
that the time had come for them to receive
the Torah she'b'al peh out of love,
"They accepted it anew in the days of Achashverosh,"
that is, the Torah she'b'al peh,
for regarding it there had been
the holding of the mountain over them like a barrel
in Hashem — "this is Torah," the Torah she'b'al peh —
as we have said many times.
שֶׁאָז הָיָה הַתְחָלַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
For then was the beginning of the Torah she'b'al peh
through the Men of the Great Assembly;
and against this came Haman's ascendancy,
who wished "to crush them and destroy them,"
and "cast a Pur, that is, the lot."
And the lot is from Heaven,
"The lot is cast into the lap,
but its every decision is from Hashem";
and the lot fell on Adar,
for in truth it was His will, Yisbarach,
to erase the memory of Amalek,
for the main erasure of Amalek
is through the Torah she'b'al peh.
And the time for this is in the month of Adar,
that the offspring of Esav is delivered
only into the hand of the offspring of Yosef;
and the month of Adar corresponds to Yosef HaTzaddik,
as written in the sefer Kedushas Levi
and likewise Yosef is sometimes counted
And for this reason it was caused
and from Heaven it fell on Adar,
in order to erase his memory in Adar;
and without the lot, who knows
settled specifically on the month of Adar.
And the Pur that fell on Adar
that even at the start of the decree
the intent was toward the erasure of Amalek,
and not, chas v'shalom, against the Jews.
And the Pur was for the salvation,
that "the Jews themselves ruled over their enemies";
and this came about through the Pur,
with which he wished "to kill and to destroy," etc.;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הָיָה פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה לְאֶסְתֵּר
and through this Esther had an opening
and to carry out the erasure of Amalek.
it would not have been relevant
for her to ask to kill them
that they rule over their enemies,
and that the first letters be reversed.
And this is the meaning of the opening with the verse
"And it shall be, as Hashem rejoiced over you
(and so it is written in the Zohar Chadash,
כִּי תָבוֹא עג, ב עַיֵּין שָׁם)
Rather, the intent of this decree
and through this there will be
the destruction of Esav and Amalek;
like the joy of "to do you good,"
דְּגַם זֶה הוּא לְהֵטִיב עוֹד יוֹתֵר
for this too is to do even more good,
as mentioned above regarding what is said,
"And it shall be, when you grieve," etc.
And therefore "vehayah" is written in both,
for it is an expression of joy.
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת לֹא יִגַּע בָּהֶם רַע
For in truth no harm will touch them,
they will have their complete downfall,
and through this Yisrael will draw closer
"Greater was the removal of the ring
And this is why they said in the Gemara the expression
"so will He rejoice to do you harm,"
instead of what is said in the verse,
based on what we find in Egypt:
the kelipah of Egypt grew stronger,
and Pharaoh abolished Shabbos from them,
and said, "And since I came to Pharaoh
he has done evil to this people" (Shemos 5:23).
That is, he made them bad,
in that he abolished from them the holiness of Shabbos
(and this was explained in Pri Tzaddik,
שְׁמוֹת מַאֲמָר ג; וָאֵרָא מַאֲמָר ז)
And so they hinted in the Gemara
with the expression "to do you harm,"
that is, the ascendancy of the idolaters,
from the holiness of Hashem Yisbarach;
for on the contrary, the severity of the decree
will cause Yisrael to draw close
as it was in the days of Haman.
And on this the Gemara asks,
at the downfall of the wicked?",
even though their downfall is just,
who were drowned measure for measure,
as they had decreed, "Cast him into the river";
HaKadosh Baruch Hu does not rejoice.
And for this it brings the derashah
of "one did not come near the other,"
that He did not allow the ministering angels
"The work of My hands is drowning in the sea," etc.;
that "for it is good" is not said in the thanksgiving
against Ammon and Moav, who pursued him.
but He causes others to rejoice,"
for it is written "so will He cause rejoicing,"
that is, He will gladden and cause Yisrael to rejoice,
so that they rejoice at their downfall,
as with Haman, as mentioned above.
And this is what they said afterwards in the Gemara
the opening "He remembered His kindness and His faithfulness
all the ends of the earth saw
"In the days of Mordechai and Esther."
For "all the ends of the earth" does not mean
since they did not recognize the miracle,
as it was close to nature,
rather, "all the ends of the earth" means
that everything came from the salvation of our God,
for it was not the way of nature
that a great king should kill his wife
because she did not obey him
and even the lesser souls recognized
that it all came from the hand of Hashem,
so that there would be the erasure of Amalek,
and to increase the holiness of Yisrael
with the light of the Torah she'b'al peh,
And certainly, had it been His will, Yisbarach,
to erase the memory of Amalek entirely,
He could have destroyed him in an instant;
however, it is His will, Yisbarach,
that the war be "from generation to generation,"
that in every generation Yisrael grow strong
to uproot the kelipah of Amalek
and I erase his name above";
that is, it is His will, Yisbarach,
that in every generation Yisrael fight
and defeat it with the help of Hashem,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִזְכּוּ אַחַר כָּךְ
and through this they will afterwards merit
and the complete erasure of Amalek,
"and there will be no survivor," etc.
And this is what they said (Megillah 7b):
"A person is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim
For it is written in Pri Etz Chaim
that there is a spark of holiness
in every kelipah that gives it life,
and if it were removed from it,
no vitality would remain for it,
and it would be completely nullified at once;
from the illumination of this day,
but not that it reach so far
and therefore a person is obligated to become intoxicated
and perhaps out of the intoxication
that spark within the kelipah will also be blessed,
but it will not be a complete blessing
it would shine also upon the kelipah;
And because it was blessed by mistake,
there is strength in the Jewish souls
to defeat it, to overpower it,
for the blessing was by mistake,
And in truth, even at the time of intoxication,
they begin with words of Torah
and only in error did the blessing go forth
and therefore we have the strength
to fight against him and defeat him
and to erase the memory of Amalek.

paragraphs.text: Esther 9:24–26 — “Haman son of Hammedasa the Agagite, enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, casting pur—that is, the lot—to confound and destroy them. But when it came before the king, he said by letter that the evil plot Haman had plotted against the Jews should return upon his own head; they hanged him and his sons on the tree. Therefore they called these days Purim, after the pur.” The verses themselves place the reversal of the plot between the original lot and the naming of the days. Rav Tzadok's question asks how the instrument of danger can itself become the name of salvation.

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 116b — “Passover—because the Omnipresent passed over our ancestors' houses in Egypt, as it is said: 'You shall say: It is a Passover offering to Hashem, Who passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt.'” The name here commemorates the act of rescue itself. This is the contrast on which the maamar's question about the name Purim rests.

paragraphs.text: Pesach Haggadah, explanation of matzah — “This matzah that we eat—why? Because our ancestors' dough did not have time to become leavened before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, was revealed to them and redeemed them, as it is said: 'They baked the dough they brought out of Egypt into unleavened cakes, for it had not leavened, because they were driven out of Egypt and could not delay, and had not prepared provisions for themselves.'” Like Passover's name, the matzah is explained through the moment of deliverance. Purim's apparent reference to the prior decree therefore requires a different account.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Resisei Layla 18 — “Shabbos is fixed by Hashem, Yom Tov and Rosh Chodesh Yisrael sanctify, but Purim was chosen by the lot through Haman, selected for the erasure of Amalek: ‘from itself the axe-handle comes.’” Rav Tzadok there answers the same question with a sharper point: Amalek, who attributes all to chance, is defeated by his own lot, since “from Hashem is all its judgment.”

paragraphs.text: Megillah 10b — “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi opened his exposition from: 'As Hashem rejoiced over you to do you good, so He will cause rejoicing ... in doing you harm.' But does the Holy One, blessed be He, rejoice at the downfall of the wicked? ... Rabbi Yochanan said: The ministering angels wished to sing; the Holy One, blessed be He, said: My handiwork is drowning in the sea, and you sing? Rabbi Elazar said: He Himself does not rejoice, but He causes others to rejoice. This is precise: it says yasis, 'He will cause rejoicing,' and not yasus, 'He will rejoice.'” The proof about the omitted 'for He is good' is taken from Yehoshafat's thanksgiving in II Chronicles 20:21. The maamar's questions concern why this teaching opens the exposition of Esther and who 'others' are in that context.

paragraphs.text: Rashi, Megillah 10b, s.v. Acherim Meisis — “He causes others to rejoice—when they became liable to destruction in Haman's days, their enemies were rejoicing over them.” Rashi identifies the rejoicing others as Israel's enemies. Rav Tzadok first raises difficulties with that reading, then proposes that the others are Israel rejoicing at the reversal of the decree onto its enemies.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Acharei Mos 12 — “Rabbi Berchyah the priest said: See what is written: 'Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion ... behold, your King comes to you, righteous and saved.' It does not say 'righteous and a savior,' but 'righteous and saved.' ... As it were, He is saved. Rabbi Meir said: 'Hashem saved Israel on that day'—as it were, He is redeemed with Israel. Whenever Israel are redeemed, it is as though He is redeemed.” The Midrash explicitly reads Israel's salvation as the Divine salvation. Rav Tzadok cites it to show why rejoicing in Israel's destruction would be impossible, even before the Gemara's proof from the drowning Egyptians.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 29a — “Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says: Come and see how beloved Israel are before the Holy One, blessed be He: wherever they were exiled, the Divine Presence was with them. They were exiled to Egypt, and the Divine Presence was with them; they were exiled to Bavel, and the Divine Presence was with them. When they are destined to be redeemed, the Divine Presence is with them, as it is said: 'Hashem your God shall return with your captivity.' It does not say 'He shall bring back,' but 'He shall return'—the Holy One, blessed be He, returns with them from the exiles.” The textual contrast between veshev and veheshiv makes the Divine Presence a participant in exile and return. It supplies the direct rabbinic premise for the maamar's argument about Divine grief and joy.

paragraphs.text: Rashi, Genesis 1:1, s.v. Bereishis Bara — “As our Sages expounded: For the sake of the Torah, which is called 'the beginning of His way,' and for the sake of Israel, who are called 'the beginning of His produce.'” Rashi's two readings of bereishis underlie the claim that Creation's purpose is bound to Torah and Israel. The Sinai condition discussed in Shabbos 88a then gives that purpose its explicit covenantal form.

paragraphs.text: Rashi, Genesis 27:40, s.v. Tarid — “Tarid is an expression of distress, as in 'I am restless in my complaint.' That is: When Israel transgress the Torah, and you have grounds to be distressed about the blessings he took, then 'you shall break his yoke' from your neck.” Rashi connects Esav's release with Israel's failing. The teaching Rav Tzadok reports from his master reads tarid additionally through Esav's own descent: its final assault precedes its fall. The two readings should be distinguished.

paragraphs.text: Bereishis Rabbah 42:3 — “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman made the distinction: Wherever vayehi is said, it denotes distress; vehayah denotes joy. They challenged him: But it is written, 'And there was light'! He replied: That too was not complete joy, for the world did not merit to use that light.” The Midrash proceeds through objections and answers to this rule. Rav Tzadok uses the proposed association of vehayah with joy when interpreting 'When you descend, you shall break his yoke.'

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Yisrael Kedoshim 7 — “‘When you break loose (tarid)’: at the end of descent you shake off his yoke—your downfall … though Hashem does not rejoice at the fall of the wicked, at Amalek's fall He surely rejoices.” Rav Tzadok there joins the same two points as his Rebbe here, tarid as yeridah and “vehaya” as joy, and adds the root: throwing off Yisrael's yoke is Amalek's power within Esav, and so is always the moment of his fall.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Korach 12 — “Gog and Magog have the numerical value seventy, corresponding to the seventy nations.” This explicit numerical interpretation is the cited basis for treating the final war as a gathering of the full range of opposing national powers. Its placement before the fullest revelation of Israel's holiness is developed by Rav Tzadok.

paragraphs.text: Yoma 10a — “Rav Yehudah said in Rav's name: The son of David does not come until the wicked kingdom of Rome spreads over the entire world for nine months, as it is said: 'Therefore He shall give them over until the time when she who gives birth has given birth; the rest of his brothers shall return to the children of Israel.'” The verse is Micah 5:2 in the Hebrew numbering. The nine-month image gives the maamar its comparison of the preceding distress to the pains of birth.

paragraphs.text: Zohar Chadash, Ki Savo, on Deuteronomy 28:61 — “'Until you are destroyed'—something that will never be, for ever and ever. For the Holy One, blessed be He, has sworn never to destroy Israel for ever and ever, and their remembrance shall endure continually, as it is written: 'So shall your offspring and your name endure'; and 'If the heavens above can be measured ... .' Since He has sworn that Israel will not be destroyed, all those blows and illnesses are destined to remain hidden and covered, not emerging to harm them until the time they cease from the world—which shall never be, for ever and ever.” The original exposition reads the threat in Deuteronomy 28:61 through the oath that Israel will endure. Rav Tzadok applies the same premise to the language 'to destroy you' in 28:63. paragraphs.text: Megillah 14a — “Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said: The removal of the signet was greater than the forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses who prophesied to Israel. They did not return Israel to proper conduct, whereas removal of the signet returned them to proper conduct.” The king's transfer of his signet to Haman made the decree effective. The Gemara identifies that moment of danger as the cause of repentance; Rav Tzadok sees the enemy's apparent success itself bringing Israel closer to God.

paragraphs.text: Shemos Rabbah 5:18 — “'Let the labor become heavy upon the men'—this teaches that they possessed scrolls with which they delighted themselves from Shabbos to Shabbos, saying that the Holy One, blessed be He, would redeem them, for they rested on Shabbos. Pharaoh said: Let the work become heavy upon the men, so that they do it and do not turn to false words—let them not delight themselves and let them not rest on Shabbos.” The Midrash explicitly connects Pharaoh's intensified labor with suppressing Shabbos rest and the sustaining scrolls of redemption. Rav Tzadok therefore reads 'he has done evil to this people' as an assault on their holiness as well as on their physical condition.

paragraphs.text: Pri Tzaddik, Va’eira §7 — “Although it was first written, 'The people believed,' that came through the power of Shabbos, which placed faith in their hearts. Shabbos is the aspect of complete faith, and through the scrolls with which they would delight from Shabbos to Shabbos, they knew that Hashem would redeem them. Once Pharaoh said, 'Let the work be heavy ... and let them not turn aside'—let them not delight and let them not rest on Shabbos—then, although Moshe Rabbeinu told them all the expressions of redemption, 'I shall take you out, save you, redeem you, and take you,' it did not enter Israel's hearts, because they lacked Shabbos and the scrolls that had brought complete faith into their hearts.” The earlier maamar explains how abolishing their Shabbos rest undermined the people's receptivity to the promised redemption. Shemos §3, also cited here and checked in its original, describes the same loss of complete faith and compares the darkening immediately before rescue to the birth-pangs of Mashiach. These are the precise background teachings for the present interpretation of Pharaoh's harm.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavos Charutz 5 — “Above, how can war apply at all, when everything is in His hand? The war is only in the heart of man … Hashem's help is His war against Amalek.” Rav Tzadok there explains why Amalek is fought “from generation to generation” and not erased at once: the battle is Yisrael's own inner struggle, won only with Divine help.

paragraphs.text: Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaPurim, chapter 6 — “On this great day, when there is that great illumination, we wish life from this illumination to reach even that spark itself, but not to such a degree that it illumines the kelippah. Therefore a person becomes intoxicated on this day until he does not distinguish 'cursed is Haman' from 'blessed is Mordechai'; perhaps he will err and give a blessing to that spark within the kelippah, so that it too is blessed. But it must not be a blessing with complete intention, for then too much would reach it and the kelippah would also be blessed.” The preceding paragraph states that every kelippah lives through a holy spark, and would immediately cease if that spark were removed. The distinction here is between sustaining the spark and sustaining the opposing shell; the maamar's subsequent account of Israel's power to overcome it depends on that distinction.
